introduction: Fasting (Tapa) is the most powerful spiritual practice in Jainism. It is not mere physical austerity — it is conscious karmic purification. By voluntarily restraining the body's needs, the aspirant destroys karmic matter, gains self-mastery, and accelerates the journey to liberation. Fasting is the fire that burns karmic fuel.

typesOfFasts.name: Upvas
typesOfFasts.description: Complete fast from food and water for 24-48 hours or longer. The most intense form of Tapas. Performed on Paryushan, Samvatsari, and other holy days.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Healthy adults and youth with prior fasting experience. Not for beginners, children, elderly, pregnant women, or the ill.

typesOfFasts.name: Chauvihar
typesOfFasts.description: 24-hour fast from both food and water. Considered the minimum complete fast. Performed by monks/nuns daily after noon; by laypeople on auspicious days.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Monks and lay practitioners following Pachchakhan vow.

typesOfFasts.name: Ekaashana
typesOfFasts.description: Eating one meal per day before sunset. All consuming stops after that single meal. Develops discipline while maintaining householder responsibilities.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: All lay Jains seeking greater discipline.

typesOfFasts.name: Beasana
typesOfFasts.description: Eating two meals per day (morning and afternoon), no evening meal. A lighter fast that creates space for evening spiritual practice.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Lay Jains beginning their fasting practice.

typesOfFasts.name: Ayambil
typesOfFasts.description: Eating only boiled food without spices, oil, ghee, or vegetables. Only one type of grain or pulses is consumed. Intensely purifying, often done during Navpad Oli.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Serious lay practitioners and monks during special periods.

typesOfFasts.name: Proshadhopavasa
typesOfFasts.description: Fasting on the 8th, 14th, and 15th days of each lunar fortnight. Eating only pure, sattvic food on these days, with intensified meditation and Pratikramana.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Householders who have taken Shikshavratas (4th vow).

typesOfFasts.name: Varshitap
typesOfFasts.description: The year-long fast commemorating Lord Rishabhdev's 400-day fast. Practitioners alternate days of eating and fasting, consuming food only on alternate days or once-daily before sunset.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Only healthy, experienced practitioners under spiritual guidance. Culminates on Akshay Tritiya.

typesOfFasts.name: Santhara / Sallekhana
typesOfFasts.description: The voluntary, gradual fasting unto death at the end of life. A deeply spiritual practice of complete renunciation of the body, undertaken only by those who are incurably ill, aged, or facing certain death. It is an act of supreme equanimity and spiritual independence.
typesOfFasts.whoShouldDo: Only when death is imminent and unavoidable. Requires strict supervision by the Sangha, Guru approval, and complete mental equanimity.

guidelines: Always begin with shorter fasts (Beasana) before attempting longer ones (Upvas)
Recite Pachchakhan (formal vow) before every fast to sanctify intention
Break fasts with light, easily digestible food (usually boiled water or fruit)
Do not break a fast under emotional pressure — the vow must be kept
Fasting days are for intensive spiritual practice, not social events or work
Listen to your body — if illness arises, break the fast without guilt
Consult an Acharya or experienced Upadhyaya for fasts longer than 3 days
safetyTips: Stay hydrated on non-fasting days to build reserves
Avoid extreme exercise during fasting periods
Children under 12, pregnant women, nursing mothers, and those with chronic illness should not fast
Elderly practitioners should consult a doctor and spiritual guide before extended fasts
Reduce work and social obligations on fasting days
Carry glucose water if you feel dizzy — breaking a fast for health is acceptable
Do not compare your fasting capacity with others — spiritual progress is personal
Breaking a fast due to genuine need is not a failure; it is wisdom
spiritualSignificance: Fasting (Tapa) destroys karma through deliberate self-restraint. Unlike passively waiting for karmic fruit, fasting actively burns karmic matter before it manifests. It develops the 3foldTap: physical (body), verbal (speech), and mental (thought). In Jainism, fasting is not asceticism for its own sake — it is the most direct method of transforming the soul from karmic bondage to liberation. It creates Viveka (discrimination), Vairagya (detachment), and Mumukshutva (intense longing for liberation).
whoShouldNotFast: Persons with diabetes, heart disease, or other serious medical conditions
Those with eating disorders or mental health conditions
Persons traveling in extreme temperatures or physical stress
Those who have not built up fasting capacity gradually
